::: {.prose}

In 2008 and 2009, BC provincial fisheries staff sampled 30 lake trout populations, from larger exploited lakes to pristine backcountry and high-alpine lakes. They collected back-calculated size-at-age from 1,100 fish. These fish varied enormously in maximum size, with several over 100 cm in fork length, and in age, with many born in the 1950s.

Throughout their range, lake trout have large- and small-bodied morphs, typically linked to diet or post-glacial evolution. These polymorphs may represent a unique contribution to both fisheries and biodiversity conservation.

## Questions we're asking

- Are polymorphs present in these 30 lakes, and if so, how many morphs are there? We use a bioenergetic somatic growth model to ask whether a fish belongs to one morph or another.
- What drives variation in growth over time? We use time-series of climate and fishery infrastructure development to find when, by age or by year, growth conditions changed.
